# Venus Williams Trades Tennis Whites for Swimwear in New Photo Shoot

(CNN) -- Fans typically picture Venus Williams drenched in sweat as she powers through intense matches on the tennis court. But a fresh set of images set to appear in Italian Marie Claire captures her in an entirely different light—relaxed and contemplative, taking a dip in the pool instead of chasing down aces.

The world's sixth-ranked player appears throughout a 16-page fashion feature for the magazine's Italian edition, with photographs captured last December in Miami by longtime friend and photographer Koto Bolofo.

"Working with Koto is something I really enjoy," Williams shared during an interview with CNN for "Revealed." "He might be my number one supporter—I honestly don't know what he sees in me, but since he believes in me that much, I figure I should just go with it," she added with a laugh.

The photo session was ambitious, cramming 20 different outfit changes into a single day. One particular shot, however, represented a concept Bolofo had been envisioning for two full years.

*See video of the photo shoot »*

"The image in my head has always been her playing tennis while submerged in water," Bolofo explained to CNN. Once clouds cleared and sunlight broke through, he had Williams change into swimwear.

"This underwater tennis concept is a first for me, so there's definitely some nervousness—but I think it'll work out fine," Williams remarked.

Bolofo wanted the final result to feel effortless. "The goal is for her to look genuinely happy, like this comes naturally to her rather than being forced," he said. "We're going for something playful and lighthearted—that's really the enjoyable part of doing this shoot."

## Fashion Runs Deep

Style holds real significance in Williams' world beyond the court. She founded EleVen, her own apparel brand that creates both tennis wear and everyday casual clothing. While she contributes sketches and concepts, Williams is quick to clarify she doesn't handle the actual design work single-handedly.

"Other designers handle the technical side—I couldn't manage that alone," she noted. "Technical drawing was never my thing; I dreaded it back in school. And I won't touch computer design programs—hand-drawing is much more my speed."

Her prominent standing among elite tennis players gives Williams a natural platform to promote her brand, which she frequently sports during matches. Beyond fashion, she also runs V Starr Interiors, an interior design firm she launched when she was barely in her twenties.

## Fame Isn't the Goal

Despite juggling multiple business ventures publicly, Williams insists her motivations lie elsewhere. "Chasing fame has never been what drives me. Winning championships and excelling at tennis—that's always been my real focus. I don't actively work to build my celebrity status," she explained.

This grounded demeanor has won her admirers far outside athletic circles. Rapper Wyclef Jean, for instance, dedicated an entire song to her last year titled "I'm Ready."

*Listen to the song »*

"It's similar to how a painter finds their muse," Jean described to CNN. "Certain people just inspire me to write music about them... I called her Venus, ruler of the universe."

The tribute delighted Williams. "I've saved every version—all the instrumentals, different mixes, various cuts. I'm a huge fan of it," she told CNN.

## Looking Ahead

This week finds Williams competing again, this time at the Barclays Dubai Tennis Championships, where she'll be aiming for a win following a disappointing early loss at January's Australian Open.

Yet even with her competitive drive intact, Williams maintains that tennis isn't what matters most to her overall. "Without question, spiritual growth ranks as the top priority in my life. Following what God asks of me—that's a continuous lesson I'm learning every single day," she reflected.

By CNN Style Staff

Venus Williams has never been content to stay in one lane. The seven-time Grand Slam champion, who has spent more than two decades redefining power and grace on the tennis court, brought that same commanding presence to a recent photo shoot for Italian Marie Claire, where she opened up about her evolving relationship with fashion, wellness and the sport that made her a household name.

Dressed in a rotating series of bold, architectural looks for the magazine, Williams appeared entirely at home in front of the camera — no surprise for an athlete who has long straddled the worlds of sport and style. Since founding her activewear line EleVen in 2007, Williams has positioned herself not just as a tennis icon but as a designer with a distinct point of view.

"I've always believed that what you wear should make you feel powerful, whether you're stepping onto a tennis court or walking into a boardroom," Williams told the magazine. "EleVen was born out of wanting pieces that could transition between performance and everyday life. Fashion and function don't have to be separate conversations."

The shoot comes as Williams continues to balance her business ventures with her enduring presence in professional tennis — a career that has spanned generational shifts in the sport since her debut in the mid-1990s. Now in her forties, she has often spoken about longevity, both athletic and personal, as central to her identity.

"People ask me all the time when I'm going to stop," she said. "But tennis isn't just what I do — it's part of who I am. I'm still curious, I still love the competition, and I still feel like I have something to give to the game."

That philosophy of reinvention extends directly into her design work. Williams described EleVen as an extension of her competitive mindset, built around the idea that clothing should empower women to move confidently through their lives.

"When I design, I'm thinking about the woman who's juggling a workout, a meeting and a dinner afterward," Williams explained. "She doesn't have time to compromise. I want her to feel like herself in every version of her day."

Throughout the shoot, Williams's styling leaned into vibrant colors and sharp tailoring — a visual echo of her on-court presence, where her serve and net play have long been described as some of the most dominant in the sport's history. Editors at Marie Claire noted that her ease in front of the camera reflected years of experience navigating both athletic pressure and public image.

Williams, who has also spoken publicly about nutrition, autoimmune health and mental resilience, tied her approach to fashion back to a broader philosophy of self-care and confidence.

"Style is another form of self-expression, just like tennis is a form of expression," she said. "Both require discipline, and both are about knowing who you are and presenting that truth to the world."

As the shoot wrapped, Williams reflected on what continues to drive her, whether on the court or in the design studio.

"I'm still evolving," she said. "I don't think I'll ever be finished figuring out who I want to be — and honestly, that's the most exciting part."

Bolofo, celebrated for his ability to find stillness and elegance in movement, captured Williams in a way rarely seen. Underwater, gravity releases its grip. The seven-time Grand Slam champion—whose game is built on explosive serves and relentless baseline power—appears weightless, almost balletic. Fabric drifts. Hair floats in slow motion. Her tennis racket, typically an instrument of aggression, becomes something closer to a prop in an aquatic dance.

The concept plays on contrast: the sport most associated with sweat, grit, and split-second reflexes reimagined in an environment of silence and slowness. It's a visual metaphor, arguably, for Williams herself—a woman who has spent over two decades in the relentless spotlight of professional sports, yet whose public image has always carried an undercurrent of calm self-possession.

The resulting images are painterly, almost surreal, with Williams' athletic frame rendered in unfamiliar softness. It's tennis stripped of its adrenaline, replaced with something meditative.

## Beyond the Court: Building an Empire

The shoot arrives at a moment when Williams' identity has expanded well beyond her athletic résumé. While her tennis legacy—Wimbledon titles, Olympic golds, a rivalry with sister Serena that reshaped women's tennis—remains foundational, Williams has spent recent years constructing a multifaceted business portfolio that reflects her broader ambitions.

She founded **V Starr Interiors**, an interior design firm, channeling a lesser-known passion for aesthetics and space into a legitimate design practice. She also launched **EleVen**, an activewear line built around the philosophy that fashion should empower women to feel confident whether they're on the court or off it. The brand's name itself is a nod to going "one step beyond ten"—a philosophy of exceeding expectations that has clearly guided her career.

These ventures aren't vanity projects tacked onto an athlete's fame; Williams has been vocal about wanting to be taken seriously as a businesswoman, studying business and pursuing degrees even during the height of her competitive career. This underwater photo shoot, in a sense, mirrors that same instinct: taking something familiar—tennis, her most public identity—and reimagining it through a different, more artistic lens.

What makes Williams a compelling subject beyond the visual spectacle is the throughline of intention in her choices. That journey pushed her toward advocating for nutrition, rest, and self-care—values that feel quietly present in the underwater imagery, where struggle and effort are replaced by fluidity and control.

Her activism, like her business ventures, tends to operate with the same measured determination that defines her on-court demeanor—less about loud proclamations, more about sustained, structural change.

## An Image Rewritten

Photo shoots like this one function as more than promotional material; they're opportunities for athletes to control their own narrative, to show dimensions of themselves that scoreboards can't capture. For Williams, someone whose life story is so entangled with competition, ambition, and family legacy, the choice to appear submerged—still, deliberate, almost dreamlike—feels less like a departure from her identity and more like an extension of it.

The racket remains in her hand. The whites are still there. But everything else has changed. In Bolofo's lens, Venus Williams isn't fighting for a point. She's simply existing, suspended between force and stillness—much like the career and legacy she continues to shape on her own terms.
